newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African minister fears deadly secrets may get out.
newsitem.headline: S.African minister fears deadly secrets may get out.

text.p: South Africa's "truth commission" said on Friday it had sought to allay the fears of Defence Minister Joe Modise that its public hearings could lead to the uncontrolled spread of chemical warfare secrets.

Truth and Reconciliation Commission Deputy Chairman Alex Boraine said Modise had met commissioners on Thursday and raised his concerns over the planned public questioning of South Africa's top chemical war expert, Wouter Basson.
"The minister expressed concerns...in relation to international treaties, particularly the one on non- proliferation, which South Africa has signed," Boraine said.
"Understandably, he did not want information which could be prejudicial to leak out, for other people to take advantage of methods, which may or may not have been used, and use them."
Boraine said Modise also feared Basson would give details that could endanger the lives of South African intelligence agents.

"Our response was that we had no intention of endangering lives or contradicting treaties... Our job was to try to establish the policy concerning chemical and biological warfare -- was this merely a defensive mechanism, or was this an offensive policy to be used against the opponents of apartheid," he said.

Basson was in charge of research started in the 1980s into chemical and biological warfare, ostensibly to provide South Africa with ways of defending itself if its enemies used the weapons against it.

Basson was arrested earlier this year on criminal drug possession charges. According to evidence at his bail hearing, documents were found in his possession indicating that South Africa developed an offensive chemical war capacity in the apartheid years.
Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils has said President Nelson Mandela's government was concerned at one stage that Basson might be tempted to sell his knowledge abroad.
The commission began probing Basson separately after learning that he was named in a army general's report on alleged human rights abuses committed by security forces during apartheid.
No date has been set for Basson to appear before the commission. His trial is currently under way in Pretoria.
